title: The Woman at the Well
lead: Jesus starts a conversation with someone everyone else avoids, and she is the first to tell the whole town about Him.
questions: Whom do I avoid so carefully that I take the long way around, and what would happen if next time I went straight through?
How do I begin my contact with people on the outside: with a request and with listening, or with a ready-made lecture?
Which part of my past, the part everyone has seen, could become my strongest testimony?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: John writes that Jesus “had to pass through Samaria.” Geographically, He had to do no such thing: devout pilgrims went the long way around, down the Jordan Valley, adding two days to the trip rather than cross a country you simply don’t visit. That “had to” doesn’t come from a map. On the other side of that avoided territory, a person was waiting. At Jacob’s well near Sychar, at high noon, God in the flesh sits down, “weary from His journey,” and says to the woman who comes up: “Give Me a drink.” Women drew water in the morning or the evening, together; noon is the choice of a woman who would rather face the sun than her neighbors. And the request meant more than we hear: in many eyes, a Samaritan woman’s jar was permanently unclean. Jesus doesn’t begin by giving. He begins by making her needed. The first gift to someone despised is the dignity of having something to offer.

The conversation about water becomes a conversation about thirst. “Living water” meant spring water, flowing on its own, as opposed to water standing in a cistern; Jesus promises a spring inside a person, not a tank to be refilled every day. And the woman’s five husbands are five buckets of hope, each one leaving her thirsty again. He doesn’t moralize, not by a single word: He diagnoses the thirst and offers the spring. When she escapes into the dispute over the holy mountain, He neither flatters her nor settles the argument in favor of His own side: God doesn’t live on any of our mountains, and true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. And it is to her, a foreign woman with a torn-up life story, that He says plainly what He had said to no one in Judea or Galilee: “I who speak to you am He.”

The woman leaves her water jar and runs into town, and she turns her shame into an argument: “He told me everything I ever did.” If He knows everything and didn’t walk away, maybe He really is the One we’ve been waiting for. The town comes out, Jesus stays two days, and the Samaritans end with a sentence that is the goal of all evangelism: we now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves. The map of the places we avoid is a map of how unlike Jesus we are. People who get avoided don’t need a lecture. They need someone who will sit down by their well.

John writes that on His way from Judea to Galilee, Jesus “had to pass through Samaria.” Geographically, He had to do no such thing. Devout pilgrims from Galilee went to Jerusalem the long way around, down the Jordan Valley by way of Jericho, adding a good two days to the journey, partly out of dislike and partly out of prudence, since the Samaritan stretch of road could be dangerous. Going around Samaria was a norm so obvious that no one bothered to explain it. Jesus goes straight through. That “had to” doesn’t come from a map; it belongs with all of God’s other “musts” in this Gospel. In Samaria, a person was waiting for Him. The section we are walking through speaks of God coming to the avoided, and no one in the Gospels is avoided as systematically as the Samaritans: an entire people you don’t visit, plus one woman whom, as we will soon see, even her own people avoided.

sections.heading: A Well at High Noon
paragraphs: The scene has an address. The town of Sychar, next to it the field Jacob gave to Joseph, and a well bearing the patriarch’s name, still standing today beside the main north–south road. John includes a detail you couldn’t invent at a desk: once he calls the place a dug well, and once a spring. It sounds inconsistent, until you stand over the well itself, which is exactly both at once: a deep shaft cut into the rock, with living water welling up at the bottom. Jesus sits down by this well, “weary from His journey,” about the sixth hour, which is to say at high noon. Here the incarnation has its simplest illustration: God, worn out from walking, sits on the rim of a well and wants a drink. And a woman comes up with a water jar. Women drew water in the morning or the evening, in the cool of the day, together with other women; noon is the choice of a woman who would rather face the sun than her neighbors. As we will see in a moment, she had her reasons. So facing each other at the well sit a Jew and a Samaritan, a man and a woman, a Teacher and a person the town talked about in whispers. Each of those pairs is a separate wall.

sections.heading: Give Me a Drink
paragraphs: Jesus starts the conversation, and He starts it with a request. Just as yesterday in Simon’s boat: before He gives anything, He first asks. “Give Me a drink” meant more than we hear. In the eyes of many teachers of that time, Samaritan vessels were permanently unclean, and later rabbis would put it bluntly, teaching that the daughters of the Samaritans are unclean from the cradle. To ask a Samaritan woman for water from her jar was to accept defilement. So the woman’s astonishment is entirely in place: “You are a Jew… How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” There were pious men who closed their eyes when they passed a woman in the street. Jesus closed His eyes to no one. And there is something more in His request: He doesn’t begin by giving. He begins by making her needed. The first gift to a despised person is not charity but the dignity of being someone who has something to offer.

sections.heading: Living Water
paragraphs: From here the conversation turns into a game played on two levels. Jesus speaks of “living water,” which was the ordinary name for running water, spring water, as opposed to the standing water of cisterns. The woman hears plumbing: “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” But for centuries a deeper current had flowed through that language: the river flowing out of Eden, the spring coming from under the threshold of the temple in the prophet’s vision, God’s lament that His people had forsaken “the fountain of living water” and dug for themselves “broken cisterns.” Israel’s ritual piety knew the difference through and through: in the mikveh, a ritual washing was valid only in living water, and when there wasn’t enough, some was kept in a separate pool to make hand-drawn water fit for use. So Jesus is telling the woman at the well: what you’re looking for, lowering your rope into the shaft every day, exists in a form that flows on its own. “The water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.” Not a tank to be filled, but a spring of your own, inside. Then, with a single sentence, He touches the place where her life is leaking: “You have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband.” Not to humiliate her, but so that the conversation about water would become a conversation about thirst. Five marriages are five buckets of hope, and after each one she was thirsty again. Jesus doesn’t moralize about it, not by a single word. He diagnoses the thirst and offers the spring.

sections.heading: A Wound, Not a Debate
paragraphs: The woman does what all of us do when a conversation gets too close: she changes the subject to a religious dispute. “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” It’s easy to miss, but she isn’t pointing at a temple. She is pointing at an empty mountain. The sanctuary on Gerizim, a real building with priests and walls, had been destroyed a hundred and fifty years earlier by a Jewish ruler, the same one who leveled Shechem. The woman is defending a place of which only the place remained, before a descendant of those who destroyed it. This dispute was not academic. Each side had its own version of the Five Books of Moses, differing even in the wording of the commandments, and they shared the same fathers, whose inheritance was the object of a quiet war, including around this very well. Jesus’ answer is astonishing from two sides at once. He doesn’t flatter her: “Salvation is from the Jews,” He says firmly; truth is not up for social negotiation. But neither does He win the argument for His own side: “A time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. God doesn’t live on any of our mountains. It is the Father who is seeking worshipers, not addresses. Where two communities have been tallying their arguments for centuries, Jesus moves the question from “where” to “how” and “Whom.”

sections.heading: I Am He
paragraphs: Then the woman speaks of her hope: “I know that Messiah… is coming.” And Jesus answers with words that have no earlier precedent in this Gospel: “I who speak to you am He.” Consider the scale of that admission. Jesus acknowledged the messianic title only three times: here; near Caesarea Philippi, when He confirmed Peter’s confession before the Twelve; and before the court, on the day of His death. In Judea and Galilee the word “Messiah” was so charged with politics and armies that it couldn’t be spoken without the risk of an uprising. Even in Samaria, messianic hope could lead people onto the swords: a few years later an armed crowd would go up Gerizim behind a man who promised to show them the sacred vessels hidden by Moses, and Pilate would crush them with his cavalry and lose his office because of it. What’s more, the woman was waiting for someone a little different from the Messiah the Jews expected: her people looked not for a king from David’s line but for a prophet like Moses, who would explain everything. Jesus doesn’t correct her ideas about the Messiah, nor does He make her first adopt Jerusalem’s expectations. He answers the hope she actually has. So the first full “It is I” in this Gospel was spoken not before scholars or crowds, but at a well, to a foreign woman with a torn-up life story, in a country you don’t visit. God says the most important things to the people no one would have thought worth telling.

sections.heading: The Abandoned Water Jar
paragraphs: The woman leaves her water jar and runs into town. That abandoned jar is a whole commentary: she came for water and leaves with the spring; she can come back for the jar later. And in town she says something psychologically perfect: “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” A woman whose past everyone knew turns her past into an argument. What had been her shame becomes her testimony: if He knows everything and didn’t walk away, maybe He really is the One we’ve been waiting for. The town comes out after her. The Samaritans ask Him to stay, and He stays two days among people with whom a Jew doesn’t spend the night. And at the end they say a sentence that is the goal of all evangelism: “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” Her testimony brought them to the threshold; from there they went on by themselves. And the seed sown at this well would keep growing long after the sower had gone. When, years later, Philip the deacon comes to Samaria with the gospel, he will be reaping a harvest from a field Someone else had sown at high noon beside Jacob’s well. Jesus told His disciples so that very day: “One sows and another reaps.”

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story begins with a route. All the devout went around; Jesus went straight through, because on the other side of the avoided territory there was a person. Every community, ours included, has its Samaria: people and circles you don’t visit, the ones everyone knows in advance are “not our kind.” The map of the places we avoid is a map of how unlike Jesus we are. Second: Jesus talked before He taught. He asked for water, listened, answered her questions, and didn’t preach a single sermon. People who get avoided don’t need a lecture first; they need someone who will sit down by their well and ask for something only they can give. And third: the most effective evangelist in this Gospel turned out to be a woman with a life story no committee would ever have approved for a witness. God doesn’t wait to send a person until their past is fit for a display case. Sometimes it is precisely the past everyone stared at that makes the testimony impossible to refute: He told me everything I ever did, and He didn’t walk away.
